consumer_summary.what_it_is: Selina-3,7(11)-diene is a sesquiterpenoid, a class of aromatic molecules known for building the complex, earthy, and woody scents of many plants. You are most likely to encounter it in a hoppy craft beer or the distinct aroma of hemp and cannabis flowers. It contributes to the rich, volatile essential oils that give these plants their characteristic profiles.
consumer_summary.found_in: This molecule is notably found in the flowers of Humulus lupulus, the hops plant used to brew beer, as well as in the essential oils of hemp and cannabis.
consumer_summary.why_researchers_care: Researchers are drawn to selina-3,7(11)-diene to understand how the complex volatile profiles of hops and hemp might interact with human biology. They are particularly interested in its potential as an antioxidant and anti-inflammatory agent. The strongest evidence so far comes from human observational research (Oxford level 2b) looking at inflammation, alongside early animal and lab models exploring how it protects cells from oxidative stress.

structure_function.statement: Early human observational work points toward a role in supporting healthy inflammatory responses.
structure_function.basis: This rests on 2 papers, including one human observational study.

structure_function.statement: Animal research suggests it may support the body's natural antioxidant defenses.
structure_function.basis: This is based on 5 papers, including 2 animal studies.

structure_function.statement: In vitro studies indicate it is being explored for potential antimicrobial properties.
structure_function.basis: This is supported by 1 in vitro study.

hypothesized_benefits.hypothesis: Researchers are exploring whether selina-3,7(11)-diene can actively modulate inflammatory pathways, which could help explain some of the soothing properties attributed to hemp and hop extracts.
hypothesized_benefits.study_to_test_it: A randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled human trial (Oxford level 1b) administering a standardized dose of selina-3,7(11)-diene over 8 weeks, measuring systemic inflammatory markers like CRP and IL-6 in blood serum.

hypothesized_benefits.hypothesis: Early animal work points toward the possibility that this molecule helps neutralize free radicals, raising the question of whether it could protect human tissues from daily oxidative damage.
hypothesized_benefits.study_to_test_it: A human observational cohort study (Oxford level 2b) tracking dietary or occupational exposure to selina-3,7(11)-diene-rich extracts and correlating it with baseline markers of oxidative stress, such as lipid peroxidation products.

hypothesized_benefits.hypothesis: If early lab results bear out, researchers hope to understand whether this terpene can inhibit the growth of specific bacterial or fungal strains, potentially serving as a natural botanical preservative.
hypothesized_benefits.study_to_test_it: An in vivo animal model (Oxford level 5) applying a topical formulation of the molecule to superficial skin abrasions inoculated with common pathogens, measuring bacterial load reduction over 7 days.

hypothesized_benefits.hypothesis: Because it appears alongside acetylcholinesterase in the literature, researchers are exploring whether it might interact with neurological pathways to support cognitive function.
hypothesized_benefits.study_to_test_it: An in vitro study (Oxford level 5) exposing cultured human neurons to the molecule to measure its direct effect on acetylcholinesterase inhibition and cellular survival under stress.

consumer_summary.evidence_at_a_glance: Best evidence so far is human observational work (Oxford 2b); most of the rest is animal and lab research focusing on antioxidant potential.
